key_terms.meaning: Value of a state variable just before switching, at t = 0⁻, written i<sub>L</sub>(0⁻) or v<sub>C</sub>(0⁻).
Inductor current and capacitor voltage cannot jump: i<sub>L</sub>(0⁺) = i<sub>L</sub>(0⁻) and v<sub>C</sub>(0⁺) = v<sub>C</sub>(0⁻).
Steady value at t → ∞ found with L replaced by a short and C by an open for DC sources.
τ = L/R for an RL circuit and τ = RC for an RC circuit, in seconds; in one τ the response covers 63.2 % of the way from its initial to its final value.
A circuit with no independent source after t = 0, so only stored energy drives the response.
The part of the answer produced by the circuit's own stored energy and roots; it decays with time in a passive circuit.
The part of the answer fixed by the source alone; for a constant or sine source it equals the steady-state response.
Natural part plus forced part, conveniently written x(t) = x(∞) + [x(0⁺) − x(∞)]e<sup>−t/τ</sup> for a first-order circuit.
The equation that gives the natural roots; for a series RLC it is s² + (R/L)s + 1/(LC) = 0.
Overdamped = two distinct real roots, critically damped = equal real roots, underdamped = complex roots.
α = R/(2L) for a series RLC and α = 1/(2RC) for a parallel RLC, in s⁻¹ (nepers per second).
ω<sub>n</sub> = 1/√(LC) rad/s; the frequency the circuit would ring at if resistance were zero.
ζ = α/ω<sub>n</sub>, dimensionless; for a series RLC, ζ = (R/2)√(C/L).
ω<sub>d</sub> = ω<sub>n</sub>√(1 − ζ²) rad/s, the actual ringing frequency when ζ < 1.
F(s) = ∫ f(t)e<sup>−st</sup> dt from t = 0⁻ to ∞, with s = σ + jω the complex frequency.
Inductance L becomes impedance sL with a series source L i<sub>L</sub>(0⁻); capacitance C becomes 1/(sC) with a series source v<sub>C</sub>(0⁻)/s.
H(s) = Y(s)/X(s) with all independent sources killed and zero initial energy.
Poles are the roots of the denominator of H(s) and set the natural response; zeros are the roots of the numerator and set how strongly each mode and each frequency appears.
x = [i<sub>L</sub>, v<sub>C</sub>]ᵀ, the set of energy variables that completely describes the circuit at any instant.
f(0⁺) = lim s→∞ sF(s), a quick check on an inverse Laplace answer.

takeaways: Inductor current and capacitor voltage are the two quantities that cannot jump, so the circuit state at t = 0⁻ decides the whole answer after switching.
With no source, energy drains as a pure exponential e<sup>−t/τ</sup> whose speed is fixed only by R and the storage element.
Every first-order answer is final value plus (initial value minus final value) times e<sup>−t/τ</sup>; find the two end values and τ and the work is done.
Two storage elements give a quadratic characteristic equation, and its two roots decide whether the answer creeps, settles cleanly, or rings.
The pair ω<sub>n</sub> and ζ replaces R, L and C as the description of a second-order circuit: ω<sub>n</sub> sets how fast it wants to oscillate, ζ sets how fast the oscillation is killed.
With a sine source the complete response is a steady-state sine plus a decaying exponential whose size depends on the instant of switching.
The Laplace transform turns the differential equation into algebra and puts the initial conditions inside the circuit as extra sources.
With sources killed and zero initial energy the circuit is a single ratio H(s); its poles give the natural response and its zeros shape the steady-state response.
State variables turn any circuit into ẋ = Ax + Bu and y = Cx + Du, where the eigenvalues of A are the natural frequencies.
bank_note: Most syllabi ask for the solution of the first- and second-order differential equations of series and parallel RL, RC and RLC circuits with DC and sinusoidal sources, the initial and final conditions, and the Laplace transform method. A long answer usually pairs a short derivation with a numerical example and checks its result at t = 0⁺ and t → ∞.

bank.q: State the continuity conditions for an inductor and a capacitor and explain them from stored energy. Draw the equivalent of R, L and C at t = 0⁺ and at t → ∞. Then apply them: a 20 V source feeds R₁ = 4 Ω to node a; from a, C = 0.1 F goes to the return line, and so does a branch of L = 0.5 H in series with R₂ = 6 Ω. After a long time the switch opens at t = 0 and removes the source and R₁. Find i<sub>L</sub>, v<sub>C</sub>, i<sub>C</sub>, v<sub>L</sub> and both first slopes at 0⁺.
outline: i<sub>L</sub>(0⁺) = i<sub>L</sub>(0⁻) and v<sub>C</sub>(0⁺) = v<sub>C</sub>(0⁻), from W = ½Li² and ½Cv² (a jump needs infinite power)
v<sub>L</sub>, i<sub>C</sub> and every resistor quantity may jump
Equivalents: at 0⁺, L → current source i<sub>L</sub>(0⁻), C → voltage source v<sub>C</sub>(0⁻); at ∞ with DC, L → short, C → open
At 0⁺: i<sub>C</sub> = −2 A, v<sub>L</sub> = 0 V, dv<sub>C</sub>/dt = −20 V/s, di<sub>L</sub>/dt = 0 A/s
answer: Inductor. vL = L diL/dt and the stored energy is W = ½LiL². If iL jumped by Δi in zero time, W would change in zero time, which needs infinite power, and diL/dt would be infinite, so vL would be infinite. No real source supplies either, so iL(0⁺) = iL(0⁻).
Capacitor. iC = C dvC/dt and W = ½CvC². A jump in vC would need an infinite current and infinite power, so vC(0⁺) = vC(0⁻).
What may jump. The inductor voltage, the capacitor current and every resistor voltage and current. A resistor has no memory and obeys v = Ri at every instant.

Example, t < 0. DC steady state: L is a short and C is open. One current flows from the source through R₁, L and R₂: i = 20/(4 + 6) = 2 A, so iL(0⁻) = 2 A. Node a sits at the voltage across the L–R₂ branch, which is 2 × 6 = 12 V, so vC(0⁻) = 12 V.
Across the switch. iL(0⁺) = 2 A and vC(0⁺) = 12 V.

The 0⁺ circuit. With the source and R₁ gone, the loop is C, L and R₂. The inductor current of 2 A must come from the capacitor, flowing out of its + plate: iC(0⁺) = −2 A (it was 0 A at 0⁻, so it jumped).
Inductor voltage. KVL round the loop: vC = vL + R₂ iL, so vL(0⁺) = 12 − 6 × 2 = 0 V.

answer.pre:
dv<sub>C</sub>/dt (0⁺) = i<sub>C</sub>(0⁺)/C = −2/0.1 = −20 V/s
di<sub>L</sub>/dt (0⁺) = v<sub>L</sub>(0⁺)/L = 0/0.5  = 0 A/s

answer: Final values. No source is left, so all the stored energy (½ × 0.5 × 2² + ½ × 0.1 × 12² = 1 + 7.2 = 8.2 J) ends in R₂, and iL(∞) = 0, vC(∞) = 0.

answer.text: Sketch of the three pictures. Draw the circuit three times: for t < 0 with L shorted and C open (one loop, 2 A); for 0⁺ with a 2 A current source in place of L and a 12 V source in place of C; for ∞ with L shorted and C open and no source, so everything is zero.

answer: Which quantities jumped. iC went from 0 to −2 A and the current in R₁ from 2 A to 0, while iL stayed at 2 A and vC at 12 V. The resistor R₂ still carries 2 A because it is in series with the inductor.

Common slips. Treating the capacitor as a short at 0⁺ because "a capacitor is a short at switching" (true only when it holds 0 V); and taking vL(0⁺) from the old circuit, where it was 0 for a different reason (DC steady state).
Check. The capacitor starts falling at 20 V/s while the inductor current starts flat: the two first slopes are the two conditions a second-order solution needs.

bank.q: Define the time constant of an RC circuit and of an RL circuit. Derive the source-free RC response, state the meaning of one, three and five time constants, and show that the tangent at t = 0 meets the axis at t = τ.
outline: τ = RC and τ = L/R, both in seconds
RC dv/dt + v = 0 gives v = V₀e<sup>−t/τ</sup>
At τ: 36.8 % left; 3τ: 5.0 % left; 5τ: 0.67 % left, taken as settled
Tangent: slope −V₀/τ reaches zero at t = τ
answer: Definition. The time constant τ is the time in which a first-order response covers 63.2 % of the way from its initial to its final value; for a decay to zero, the value falls to 36.8 % of its start. For RC, τ = RC; for RL, τ = L/R. With R in ohms, C in farads and L in henries both come out in seconds (Ω × F = s and H/Ω = s).

answer.text: Derivation, source-free RC. A capacitor charged to V₀ is switched across R at t = 0. KCL at the top node:
answer.pre:
C dv/dt + v/R = 0
dv/v = −dt/(RC)
ln v = −t/(RC) + k,  and v(0) = V₀ gives k = ln V₀
v(t) = V₀ e<sup>−t/RC</sup> = V₀ e<sup>−t/τ</sup>

answer.text: What is left after n time constants.

answer: Meaning. After τ the response has 36.8 % left (63.2 % of the change done); after 3τ, 5.0 % left (95 % done); after 5τ, 0.67 % left (99.3 % done), which is taken as steady state in practice although it is never exactly zero.
Tangent. dv/dt at t = 0 is −V₀/τ. The tangent line is v = V₀ − (V₀/τ)t, which reaches 0 at t = τ. So τ is the time the response would take if it kept its starting rate.
Example values. R = 10 kΩ and C = 47 μF give τ = 10⁴ × 47 × 10⁻⁶ = 0.47 s, so the capacitor is practically discharged after 5τ = 2.35 s. L = 0.2 H and R = 40 Ω give τ = 0.2/40 = 5 ms.

answer.pre:
L di/dt + R i = 0
di/i = −(R/L) dt
i(t) = I₀ e<sup>−Rt/L</sup> = I₀ e<sup>−t/τ</sup>,   τ = L/R

answer: Half-life. The time to fall to half is τ ln 2 = 0.693τ; for the 0.47 s RC example that is 0.326 s.
Effect of R. In RC a larger R gives a larger τ (slower decay, smaller current); in RL a larger R gives a smaller τ (faster decay, more power i²R). Examiners often ask for this contrast.
RL by the same steps. L di/dt + Ri = 0 gives i = I₀e−Rt/L, so τ = L/R.

bank.q: Distinguish between the natural, forced and complete responses of a linear circuit. Derive the complete response of a series RC circuit switched onto a DC source V<sub>s</sub> when the capacitor already holds V₀, and apply it with V<sub>s</sub> = 12 V, V₀ = 4 V, R = 2 kΩ and C = 100 μF.
outline: Natural: source set to zero, form Ae<sup>−t/τ</sup>, set by the circuit
Forced: follows the source; for DC it is the final value
Complete = natural + forced; constant fixed by v(0⁺)
Example: τ = 0.2 s, v<sub>C</sub> = 12 − 8e<sup>−5t</sup> V, 9.06 V at t = τ
answer: Natural response. The solution of the circuit equation with every independent source set to zero. It depends only on the circuit (here the form Ae−t/τ) and dies away in a passive circuit. Also called the free, homogeneous or transient response.
Forced response. A particular solution that follows the source: a constant for a DC source, a sinusoid of the source frequency for a sine source. For DC it equals the final steady value.
Complete response. Natural + forced. The constant A in the natural part is fixed by the initial condition, which is why the complete response, not the natural part alone, must match v(0⁺).

answer.text: Derivation. KVL for t > 0 with i = C dvC/dt:
answer.pre:
RC dv<sub>C</sub>/dt + v<sub>C</sub> = V<sub>s</sub>
natural:   v<sub>n</sub> = A e<sup>−t/τ</sup>,  τ = RC
forced:    v<sub>f</sub> = V<sub>s</sub>          (constant source, dv/dt = 0)
complete:  v<sub>C</sub> = V<sub>s</sub> + A e<sup>−t/τ</sup>
t = 0⁺:    V₀ = V<sub>s</sub> + A,  so A = V₀ − V<sub>s</sub>
v<sub>C</sub>(t) = V<sub>s</sub> + (V₀ − V<sub>s</sub>) e<sup>−t/τ</sup>

answer: Answer. vC(t) = 12 − 8e−5t V. Forced part 12 V; natural part −8e−5t V.
Current. i = C dvC/dt = 100 × 10⁻⁶ × 40e−5t = 4e−5t mA. Check at 0⁺: (12 − 4)/2000 = 4 mA ✓.
Value at t = τ. vC(0.2) = 12 − 8 × 0.3679 = 9.06 V: the capacitor has covered 63.2 % of the way from 4 V to 12 V.

Sketch. Draw the forced part as a flat line at 12 V, the natural part as a curve starting at −8 V and rising to 0, and the complete response as their sum: a curve from 4 V rising towards 12 V with initial slope 8/0.2 = 40 V/s, its tangent meeting 12 V at t = τ = 0.2 s.
Same idea for RL. For a series RL circuit with I₀ = 0, Vs = 12 V, R = 4 Ω and L = 2 H: forced part 3 A, natural part −3e−2t A, complete i = 3(1 − e−2t) A, with τ = 0.5 s.
Checks. vC(0⁺) = 12 − 8 = 4 V = V₀ ✓; vC(∞) = 12 V, the open-capacitor value ✓.

bank.q: Derive the characteristic equation of a source-free series RLC circuit and show how its roots classify the response as overdamped, critically damped or underdamped. State the condition on R for the series and the parallel circuit, and illustrate with L = 0.5 H and C = 50 μF.
outline: KVL: L di/dt + Ri + (1/C)∫i dt = 0; differentiate
Roots −α ± √(α² − ω₀²); three cases with response forms
Example: series R<sub>crit</sub> = 200 Ω, parallel R<sub>crit</sub> = 50 Ω; R = 100 Ω series underdamped, ω<sub>d</sub> = 173.2 rad/s

answer.text: Equation. With no source, KVL round the series loop and one differentiation give
answer.pre:
L di/dt + R i + (1/C)∫ i dt = 0
L d²i/dt² + R di/dt + i/C = 0
try i = A e<sup>st</sup>:   L s² + R s + 1/C = 0
s² + (R/L) s + 1/(LC) = 0

answer: Standard form. s² + 2αs + ω₀² = 0 with α = R/(2L) (s⁻¹) and ω₀ = 1/√(LC) (rad/s). Roots: s₁,₂ = −α ± √(α² − ω₀²).

head: Condition
Roots
Name
Natural response
rows: e<sup>−αt</sup>(A₁ cos ω<sub>d</sub> t + A₂ sin ω<sub>d</sub> t)

answer: Condition on R, series. α = ω₀ gives R/(2L) = 1/√(LC), so Rcrit = 2√(L/C). Larger R is overdamped, smaller R is underdamped.

Condition on R, parallel. Here α = 1/(2RC), so α = ω₀ gives Rcrit = ½√(L/C). Now a smaller R is overdamped and a larger R is underdamped: the opposite of the series circuit, because a large parallel R draws little current and removes little energy.
Example. √(L/C) = √(0.5/(50 × 10⁻⁶)) = √10⁴ = 100 Ω. Series: Rcrit = 200 Ω. Parallel: Rcrit = 50 Ω. Also ω₀ = 1/√(0.5 × 50 × 10⁻⁶) = 1/0.005 = 200 rad/s.

One case worked. Series with R = 100 Ω: α = 100/(2 × 0.5) = 100 s⁻¹ < ω₀ = 200 rad/s, so underdamped, with ωd = √(200² − 100²) = 173.2 rad/s and ζ = α/ω₀ = 0.5. The same R in parallel gives α = 1/(2 × 100 × 50 × 10⁻⁶) = 100 s⁻¹ as well (because R = √(L/C) here), also underdamped.

answer.text: The other two series cases for this L and C.

answer: Why the overdamped one is slow. With R = 400 Ω the root −53.6 s⁻¹ has a time constant of 1/53.6 = 18.7 ms, while the critical root −200 s⁻¹ has 5 ms. More damping moves one root towards the origin, so the response creeps.
Physical picture. In the underdamped case energy swings between L and C faster than R can remove it, so the current reverses; in the overdamped case R removes it before it can swing back.

Root locus in words. As R rises from 0 the two roots start on the jω axis at ±j200, move left along a circle of radius ω₀ = 200 rad/s, meet at −200 when R = 200 Ω, and then split along the real axis, one towards the origin and one towards −∞.
Sketches. Overdamped: a slow, monotonic approach. Critical: the fastest approach without overshoot. Underdamped: an overshoot and decaying ringing inside the envelope e−αt.

bank.q: A 100 V DC source has charged a 20 μF capacitor through a 50 kΩ resistor for a long time. At t = 0 the switch moves so that the capacitor is disconnected from the source and discharges through the same 50 kΩ resistor. Find v<sub>C</sub>(t), i(t), the time constant, the time for the capacitor to fall to 20 V, and the energy dissipated in the resistor.
outline: v<sub>C</sub>(0⁻) = 100 V (C open in steady state), continuity gives v<sub>C</sub>(0⁺) = 100 V
v<sub>C</sub> = 100e<sup>−t</sup> V; i = 2e<sup>−t</sup> mA flowing out of the + plate
Energy ½CV₀² = 0.1 J, all into R
answer: Before the switch. In DC steady state the capacitor is open, no current flows in the 50 kΩ resistor, and the capacitor holds the full source voltage: vC(0⁻) = 100 V.
Continuity. vC(0⁺) = 100 V. The current, however, jumps from 0 to 100/50 000 = 2 mA at 0⁺.
Time constant. τ = RC = 50 × 10³ × 20 × 10⁻⁶ = 1 s.
Voltage. Source-free decay to zero: vC(t) = 100e−t/1 = 100e−t V for t ≥ 0.

Current. Taking i as the current leaving the + plate through R: i = vC/R = 2e−t mA. In the capacitor's own reference (into the + plate) it is iC = C dvC/dt = 20 × 10⁻⁶ × (−100e−t) = −2e−t mA, the same current with the sign of discharge.

answer.pre:
100 e<sup>−t</sup> = 20
e<sup>−t</sup> = 0.2
t = ln 5 = 1.609 s

answer: Energy. Stored at t = 0: ½CV₀² = ½ × 20 × 10⁻⁶ × 100² = 0.1 J. Dissipated in R: ∫ i²R dt = (V₀²/R)(τ/2) = (10⁴/(5 × 10⁴)) × 0.5 = 0.1 J, the whole stored energy.

answer.text: Equation for t > 0. KCL at the top of the capacitor, with no source:
answer.pre:
C dv<sub>C</sub>/dt + v<sub>C</sub>/R = 0
dv<sub>C</sub>/dt = −v<sub>C</sub>/(RC) = −v<sub>C</sub>/τ
v<sub>C</sub>(t) = v<sub>C</sub>(0⁺) e<sup>−t/τ</sup>

answer: Power at the start. p(0⁺) = V₀²/R = 100²/50 000 = 0.2 W, falling as e−2t, twice as fast as the voltage.

answer.pre:
W<sub>R</sub> = ∫ (v<sub>C</sub>²/R) dt  from 0 to ∞
    = (V₀²/R) ∫ e<sup>−2t/τ</sup> dt = (V₀²/R)(τ/2)
    = 0.2 × 0.5 = 0.1 J

answer: Sketch. vC falls from 100 V along an exponential whose tangent at t = 0 meets zero at t = 1 s; it passes 36.8 V at 1 s and 20 V at 1.61 s.
Half-voltage time. vC = 50 V at t = τ ln 2 = 0.693 s.
Energy left in the capacitor. WC(t) = ½C vC² = 0.1e−2t J. At t = 1 s only 0.0135 J (13.5 %) is left, so 86.5 % has already gone into the resistor.
Effect of a larger resistor. With 100 kΩ, τ = 2 s and the 20 V point moves to 2 ln 5 = 3.22 s, but the resistor still absorbs 0.1 J in the end: R sets how fast the energy goes, not how much.
Common slips. Writing vC = 100(1 − e−t), the charging form, for a discharge; taking the current as 0 at 0⁺ because it was 0 at 0⁻; and leaving τ in kΩ × μF without the powers of ten.
Checks. vC(0⁺) = 100 V ✓; vC(∞) = 0 ✓; at t = τ = 1 s the voltage is 36.8 V, 36.8 % of the start ✓.

bank.q: A 10 Ω resistor and a 2 H inductor are suddenly connected to a 20 V battery at t = 0, with i<sub>L</sub>(0⁻) = 0. Find i<sub>L</sub>(t), the inductor voltage, the time for the current to reach 1 A, and the energy stored at t = 1 s.
answer: End values. i(0⁺) = i(0⁻) = 0 A. At t → ∞ the inductor is a short: i(∞) = 20/10 = 2 A.
Time constant. τ = L/R = 2/10 = 0.2 s, so 1/τ = 5 s⁻¹.

answer.pre: i<sub>L</sub>(t) = 2 + (0 − 2) e<sup>−5t</sup> = 2(1 − e<sup>−5t</sup>) A

answer: Differential-equation check. L di/dt + Ri = 20 → 2 × 10e−5t + 10 × 2(1 − e−5t) = 20e−5t + 20 − 20e−5t = 20 ✓.
Inductor voltage. vL = L di/dt = 2 × 10e−5t = 20e−5t V. At 0⁺ it is 20 V: the whole battery voltage, since the resistor carries no current yet. At ∞ it is 0.
Current at 1 s. i(1) = 2(1 − e−5) = 2(1 − 0.00674) = 1.987 A (t = 5τ, so 99.3 % of the final value).
Energy at 1 s. W = ½Li² = 0.5 × 2 × 1.987² = 3.95 J. The final stored energy is ½ × 2 × 2² = 4 J.

answer.pre:
L di/dt + R i = V
di/(V/R − i) = (R/L) dt
−ln(V/R − i) = (R/L)t + k,   i(0) = 0 gives k = −ln(V/R)
i(t) = (V/R)(1 − e<sup>−Rt/L</sup>) = 2(1 − e<sup>−5t</sup>) A

answer: Energy from the battery. In the end the inductor holds 4 J, but the battery has also supplied the heat lost in R while the current rose. That is why the energy stored at 1 s (3.95 J) is less than the battery output up to 1 s.
Sketch. i rises from 0 towards 2 A with initial slope 20/2 = 10 A/s (the tangent meets 2 A at t = τ = 0.2 s); vL falls from 20 V to 0 along the mirror-image curve.
Battery energy up to 1 s. Ws = ∫ 20 i dt = 40[t − (1 − e−5t)/5] from 0 to 1 = 40 × 0.8013 = 32.05 J. Of this, 3.95 J is stored in L and 28.11 J has become heat in R.
Effect of a larger inductor. With L = 4 H, τ = 0.4 s and the 1 A point moves to 0.4 ln 2 = 0.277 s; the final current is still 20/10 = 2 A, because L does not appear in the DC steady state.
Common slips. Writing τ = RL or R/L; starting the current at 2 A instead of 0; and using ½Li² with the final current when the question asks for the energy at a given time.
Check. At every t, Ri + vL = 20 V: at t = 0.2 s, 12.64 + 7.36 = 20 ✓.

bank.q: A series RLC circuit has R = 5 Ω, L = 1 H and C = 0.25 F and is switched onto a 10 V DC source at t = 0 with zero initial energy. Find α, ω₀ and ζ, classify the response, and find i(t), v<sub>C</sub>(t) and the peak current.
outline: α = 2.5 s⁻¹, ω₀ = 2 rad/s, ζ = 1.25: overdamped
Peak 1.575 A at t = ln 4/3 = 0.462 s
answer: Parameters. α = R/(2L) = 5/2 = 2.5 s⁻¹. ω₀ = 1/√(LC) = 1/√0.25 = 2 rad/s. ζ = α/ω₀ = 1.25 > 1: overdamped.
Form. With a DC source the final current is 0 (C open), so the current has no forced part: i(t) = A₁e−t + A₂e−4t.
Initial conditions. i(0⁺) = iL(0⁻) = 0. At 0⁺, vC = 0 and Ri = 0, so vL(0⁺) = 10 V and di/dt(0⁺) = 10/1 = 10 A/s.
Current. i(t) = (10/3)(e−t − e−4t) A.
Capacitor voltage. vC = 10 + B₁e−t + B₂e−4t with vC(0) = 0 and dvC/dt(0) = i(0)/C = 0: B₁ + B₂ = −10 and −B₁ − 4B₂ = 0, so B₁ = −40/3 and B₂ = 10/3. vC(t) = 10 − (40/3)e−t + (10/3)e−4t V.
Cross-check. C dvC/dt = 0.25 × ((40/3)e−t − (40/3)e−4t) = (10/3)(e−t − e−4t) = i ✓.

answer.pre:
L di/dt + R i + v<sub>C</sub> = 10
L C d²v<sub>C</sub>/dt² + R C dv<sub>C</sub>/dt + v<sub>C</sub> = 10
0.25 v<sub>C</sub>″ + 1.25 v<sub>C</sub>′ + v<sub>C</sub> = 10   →   s² + 5s + 4 = 0,  s = −1, −4

answer: Reading. The current rises, peaks at 1.575 A and dies out as the capacitor charges; vC climbs to 10 V without overshoot. The slow root −1 sets the long tail (time constant 1 s), the fast root −4 the early curvature.
Inductor voltage. vL = L di/dt = (10/3)(−e−t + 4e−4t) V. At 0⁺ it is (10/3) × 3 = 10 V ✓, and it changes sign at t = 0.462 s, the instant the current peaks.
Energy. In the end the capacitor holds ½CV² = ½ × 0.25 × 10² = 12.5 J. The source has moved the charge CV = 2.5 C through 10 V, supplying 25 J, so 12.5 J was lost in R: half, whatever the value of R.
Critical damping for comparison. R = 2√(L/C) = 4 Ω gives a repeated root −2, i = 10te−2t A, with a peak of 10 × 0.5 × e−1 = 1.84 A at 0.5 s: a higher, earlier peak than the overdamped 1.575 A.
Common slips. Adding a forced part 10/5 = 2 A to the current (a series capacitor blocks DC, so the final current is 0); and taking di/dt(0⁺) = 0 instead of vL(0⁺)/L.
Checks. i(0) = 0 ✓, i(∞) = 0 ✓, vC(0) = 10 − 13.33 + 3.33 = 0 ✓, vC(∞) = 10 V ✓. No overshoot, as an overdamped circuit should behave.

bank.q: An RL circuit with R = 4 Ω and L = 1 H is connected at t = 0 to v(t) = 20 sin(100t + 30°) V, with zero initial current. Find the complete current, identify the transient and steady-state parts, and estimate the first peak of the current.
outline: First peak ≈ 0.352 A at t ≈ 25.8 ms, 1.76 times the steady peak
answer: Steady-state current. Im = 20/100.08 = 0.1998 A, lagging the voltage by θ: iss(t) = 0.1998 sin(100t + 30° − 87.71°) = 0.1998 sin(100t − 57.71°) A.
Transient form. The natural part of an RL circuit is Ke−t/τ with τ = L/R = 0.25 s, so it is Ke−4t.

answer.text: Constant K. The inductor current is continuous, so i(0⁺) = 0:

answer: Complete response. i(t) = 0.1998 sin(100t − 57.71°) + 0.169e−4t A. Steady-state part: the sine. Transient part: 0.169e−4t A, which dies away in about 5τ = 1.25 s.

First peak. The period is 2π/100 = 62.8 ms, much shorter than τ, so the offset has hardly decayed when the sine first peaks. That happens when 100t − 57.71° = 90°, at t = 147.71° = 2.578 rad, so t = 25.8 ms. There the offset is 0.169e−0.103 = 0.152 A, and the total is about 0.1998 + 0.152 = 0.352 A.

Meaning. The first peak is about 1.76 times the steady peak. A nearly inductive circuit (θ close to 90°) switched near a voltage zero crossing behaves like this: it is the origin of the large first-cycle current of transformers and motors.

answer.pre:
L di/dt + R i = 20 sin(100t + 30°)
natural:  L di/dt + R i = 0  →  K e<sup>−4t</sup>
forced:   a sinusoid at 100 rad/s, found with phasors:
          I = 20∠30° / (4 + j100) = 0.1998∠−57.71° A

answer: Common slips. Using the source phase 30° in place of the current phase 30° − 87.71°; forgetting the transient term; and writing K = 0 because "the source is zero at t = 0" (here it is not, and in any case K depends on iss(0), not on the source).

Switching angles for this circuit. No transient when φ = θ = 87.71°. The largest transient when φ − θ = −90°, φ = −2.29°: then iss = −0.1998 cos 100t and K = 0.1998 A, and at the first peak t = π/100 = 31.4 ms the current reaches 0.1998 + 0.1998e−0.126 = 0.376 A, 1.88 times the steady peak.
Why the offset lasts. τ = 0.25 s is about four periods long, so the offset stays large for several cycles; in a circuit with τ shorter than a period it would hardly show.
Check. i(0) = −0.1690 + 0.1690 = 0 ✓, and as t → ∞ only the 0.1998 A sine remains ✓.

bank.q: Use the Laplace transform to find i(t) and v<sub>C</sub>(t) in a series RC circuit with R = 2 Ω and C = 0.5 F, where v<sub>C</sub>(0⁻) = 5 V, switched at t = 0 onto a 10 V source. Verify the answer with the initial and final value theorems.
outline: s-domain: source 10/s, R = 2, capacitor 1/(sC) = 2/s with series source 5/s
IVT 5 V, FVT 10 V; τ = RC = 1 s
answer: Initial state. vC(0⁻) = 5 V, with its + plate where the source will charge it. The loop current before the switch is 0.
Transformed circuit. The 10 V step becomes 10/s. R stays 2 Ω. The capacitor becomes the impedance 1/(sC) = 1/(0.5s) = 2/s in series with a source vC(0⁻)/s = 5/s that opposes the charging current.
Current. i(t) = 2.5e−t A for t ≥ 0. At 0⁺ this is 2.5 A = (10 − 5)/2 ✓.
Time answer. vC(t) = 10 − 5e−t V.

answer.pre:
sV<sub>C</sub>(s) = 10 − 5s/(s + 1)
s → ∞:  10 − 5 = 5 V  = v<sub>C</sub>(0⁺) ✓
s → 0:  10 − 0 = 10 V = v<sub>C</sub>(∞) ✓   (the only pole of sV<sub>C</sub>(s) is −1, in the left half-plane)

answer: Time-domain check. τ = RC = 2 × 0.5 = 1 s, and the first-order formula gives vC = 10 + (5 − 10)e−t = 10 − 5e−t V, the same answer.

answer.text: Same result straight from the differential equation. KVL in time: R i + vC = 10 with i = C dvC/dt, so RC dvC/dt + vC = 10. Transform it with the derivative rule:

answer: Why the two routes agree. The series source 5/s in the transformed circuit is exactly the −vC(0⁻) term of the derivative rule moved into the circuit, so the circuit route is the equation route drawn as a picture.
Sketch. vC rises from 5 V to 10 V with τ = 1 s; i falls from 2.5 A to 0 with the same τ.
Current from the voltage. i = C dvC/dt = 0.5 × 5e−t = 2.5e−t A, the same as from I(s) ✓.

Energy balance. The capacitor goes from ½ × 0.5 × 5² = 6.25 J to ½ × 0.5 × 10² = 25 J, a gain of 18.75 J. The source supplies ∫ 10 i dt = 10 × 2.5 = 25 J, and the resistor takes ∫ i²R dt = 6.25 × 2 × 0.5 = 6.25 J; 18.75 + 6.25 = 25 J ✓.
Common slips. Forgetting the initial-voltage source 5/s, which gives i = 5e−t A; and applying the final value theorem to VC(s) instead of sVC(s).

bank.q: A parallel RLC circuit has R = 10 Ω, L = 1 H and C = 0.01 F. At t = 0 the capacitor voltage is 10 V and the inductor current is zero, and there is no source. Find α, ω₀ and the damping case, the voltage v(t), and v at t = 0.1 s.
outline: α = 1/(2RC) = 5 s⁻¹, ω₀ = 10 rad/s: underdamped, ω<sub>d</sub> = 8.66 rad/s
answer: Parameters. For a parallel RLC, α = 1/(2RC) = 1/(2 × 10 × 0.01) = 5 s⁻¹ and ω₀ = 1/√(LC) = 1/√0.01 = 10 rad/s.
Case. α < ω₀, so underdamped, with ωd = √(100 − 25) = √75 = 8.66 rad/s and ζ = 0.5.

answer.text: Equation. KCL at the top node, all currents leaving:
answer.pre:
v/R + i<sub>L</sub> + C dv/dt = 0,   with di<sub>L</sub>/dt = v/L
differentiate:  C d²v/dt² + (1/R) dv/dt + v/L = 0
s² + s/(RC) + 1/(LC) = 0   →   s² + 10s + 100 = 0,  s = −5 ± j8.66

answer: Form. v(t) = e−5t(B₁ cos 8.66t + B₂ sin 8.66t).
First condition. v(0⁺) = v(0⁻) = 10 V, so B₁ = 10.
Second condition. From KCL at 0⁺: C dv/dt = −(v/R + iL) = −(10/10 + 0) = −1 A, so dv/dt(0⁺) = −1/0.01 = −100 V/s.
Answer. v(t) = e−5t(10 cos 8.66t − 5.77 sin 8.66t) V.

answer.text: Inductor current. From KCL, iL = −(v/R + C dv/dt). Working this out:
answer.pre:
C dv/dt = e<sup>−5t</sup>(−cos 8.66t − 0.577 sin 8.66t)
v/R     = e<sup>−5t</sup>(cos 8.66t − 0.577 sin 8.66t)
i<sub>L</sub>(t)  = 1.155 e<sup>−5t</sup> sin 8.66t  A

answer: Checks on iL. iL(0) = 0 ✓, and diL/dt(0) = 1.155 × 8.66 = 10 A/s = v(0)/L ✓.
Amplitude-phase form. √(10² + 5.77²) = 11.55 and tan⁻¹(5.77/10) = 30°, so v(t) = 11.55e−5t cos(8.66t + 30°) V.
Timing. The damped period is 2π/8.66 = 0.726 s, and v first crosses zero when 8.66t + 30° = 90°, at t = 1.047/8.66 = 0.121 s.
Energy. At t = 0 the circuit holds ½Cv² = ½ × 0.01 × 10² = 0.5 J, all in C; it swings into L and back while R turns all 0.5 J into heat.
Critical resistance. For the parallel circuit Rcrit = ½√(L/C) = ½ × 10 = 5 Ω. Here R = 10 Ω is larger, so the circuit is underdamped, as found.
Common slips. Using the series α = R/(2L) for a parallel circuit, and taking dv/dt(0⁺) = 0 because iL(0) = 0: the resistor current v/R still drains the capacitor at once.

Checks. v(0) = 10 V ✓. The envelope e−5t has time constant 0.2 s, so the ringing is gone in about 1 s. Doubling R to 20 Ω would halve α to 2.5 s⁻¹ and make it ring longer: a parallel circuit is less damped with a larger R.

bank.q: For a series RLC circuit with L = 1 H and C = 1 F driven by a 1 V step from rest, find the value of R that gives critical damping. Compare the capacitor voltage for R = 1 Ω, 2 Ω and 4 Ω: write each response, and compare overshoot and 2 % settling time. Explain the physical reason for the difference.
outline: R<sub>crit</sub> = 2√(L/C) = 2 Ω; ω₀ = 1 rad/s, ζ = R/2
R = 1: v = 1 − e<sup>−0.5t</sup>(cos 0.866t + 0.577 sin 0.866t), overshoot 16.3 % at 3.63 s
answer: Critical R. ω₀ = 1/√(LC) = 1 rad/s and α = R/(2L) = R/2. α = ω₀ gives R = 2 Ω (= 2√(L/C)). So ζ = R/2.
Conditions for every case. vC(0) = 0 and dvC/dt(0) = i(0)/C = 0; the final value is 1 V.
R = 2 Ω (ζ = 1, critical). Repeated root −1: v = 1 + (A₁ + A₂t)e−t. v(0) = 0 gives A₁ = −1, and v′(0) = A₂ − A₁ = 0 gives A₂ = −1, so v = 1 − (1 + t)e−t.
Overshoot check. 100e−πζ/√(1 − ζ²) = 100e−1.814 = 16.3 %, so the peak is 1.163 V.

Physical reason. L and C pass energy back and forth; R removes it. With small R the exchange wins, the capacitor voltage overshoots and rings, and the ringing dies inside the envelope e−αt. With large R the resistor takes the energy before it can swing back, but the slow root −0.268 makes the voltage creep. Critical damping is the balance: the fastest settling with no overshoot.

Sketch. All three start at 0 with zero slope. The 1 Ω curve rises fastest, overshoots to 1.163 V at 3.63 s and settles in about 8 s; the 2 Ω curve rises without overshoot and is within 2 % at 5.8 s; the 4 Ω curve creeps and needs about 14.9 s.
Settling of the overdamped case. The slow root −0.268 dominates, so the estimate is 4/0.268 = 14.9 s; using 4/α = 4/2 = 2 s here is a common slip.
Design note. If a little overshoot is acceptable, ζ near 0.7 settles faster still; that is why filters and control loops are often designed near ζ = 0.7.

bank.q: A sinusoidal source v = V<sub>m</sub> sin(ωt + φ) is switched onto a series RL circuit with zero initial current at t = 0. Show that the size of the transient term depends on the switching angle φ, find the angle at which there is no transient and the angle at which it is largest, and illustrate with R = 4 Ω, L = 1 H, V<sub>m</sub> = 10 V and ω = 3 rad/s.
outline: i = I<sub>m</sub> sin(ωt + φ − θ) + Ke<sup>−t/τ</sup>, I<sub>m</sub> = V<sub>m</sub>/|Z|, θ = tan⁻¹(ωL/R)
Example: θ = 36.87°, I<sub>m</sub> = 2 A; φ = 36.87° no transient; φ = −53.13° gives i = −2 cos 3t + 2e<sup>−4t</sup>
Inductive circuits: worst at the voltage zero

answer.text: Complete response. KVL: L di/dt + Ri = Vm sin(ωt + φ). Forced part by phasors, natural part from the source-free equation:
answer.pre:
i(t) = I<sub>m</sub> sin(ωt + φ − θ) + K e<sup>−t/τ</sup>
I<sub>m</sub> = V<sub>m</sub>/√(R² + ω²L²),   θ = tan⁻¹(ωL/R),   τ = L/R

answer.text: Constant. The inductor current is continuous, so i(0⁺) = 0:
answer.pre: 0 = I<sub>m</sub> sin(φ − θ) + K   →   K = −I<sub>m</sub> sin(φ − θ)

answer: Dependence on φ. K varies as sin(φ − θ): the moment of switching decides how far the steady sine is from the actual current at t = 0, and K makes up the difference.

No transient. K = 0 when sin(φ − θ) = 0, that is φ = θ (or θ + 180°): the switch closes at the instant the steady-state current would itself be passing through zero, so the current starts on its steady path.
Largest transient. |K| = Im when φ − θ = ±90°: the switch closes when the steady current would be at a peak, so the offset equals the full steady peak.
Check of the worst case. At t = 0: −2 + 2 = 0 ✓. The offset 2e−4t starts as large as the steady peak.

Does the first peak double? Only when τ is long compared with the period. Here τ = 0.25 s and the period is 2.09 s, so in the worst case the steady peak at t = π/3 = 1.05 s meets an offset of only 2e−4.19 = 0.03 A. In a nearly inductive circuit (ωL ≫ R, θ → 90°) the worst angle is φ ≈ 0, a voltage zero crossing, and the offset lasts many cycles, so the first peak approaches 2Im.

answer.pre:
Z = R + jωL = |Z|∠θ
I = (V<sub>m</sub>∠φ)/(|Z|∠θ) = I<sub>m</sub>∠(φ − θ)
i<sub>ss</sub>(t) = I<sub>m</sub> sin(ωt + φ − θ)

answer: Why the offset is a pure exponential. The natural part of a first-order RL circuit is always Ke−t/τ; it cannot oscillate, so all the switching angle can change is its size and sign.

A nearly inductive case. With R = 0.3 Ω, the same L and ω: θ = 84.3°, Im = 10/3.015 = 3.32 A and τ = 3.33 s, longer than the 2.09 s period. In the worst case the first peak at t = π/3 meets an offset of Im e−0.314 = 0.730 Im, so the current reaches 1.73 × 3.32 = 5.74 A.

Sketch. For φ = θ the current is a plain sine from the first instant. For φ − θ = −90° it is a sine riding on a decaying offset, displaced to one side of the axis, and it slides back to centre as the offset dies.
Practical meaning. Point-on-wave switching closes a breaker near φ = θ to avoid the offset; transformer inrush is the same effect made worse by core saturation.

bank.q: A series RLC circuit has R = 3 Ω, L = 1 H and C = 0.5 F, driven by v<sub>s</sub>(t). Choose state variables, write the state equations ẋ = Ax + Bu, and write the output equation for y = v<sub>L</sub>. Find the natural frequencies from A, relate them to the characteristic equation, and find the final state for a 1 V step.
answer: States. The energy variables: x₁ = iL (the loop current) and x₂ = vC. They cannot jump, and together they fix the circuit's future for a known input.
Inductor equation. KVL: vs = RiL + L diL/dt + vC, so diL/dt = −3iL − vC + vs.
Capacitor equation. KCL: C dvC/dt = iL, so dvC/dt = iL/0.5 = 2iL.
Output. vL = vs − RiL − vC = −3x₁ − x₂ + u. So C = [−3, −1] and D = [1]. D is not zero because the source appears in vL at the same instant; for y = vC it would be C = [0, 1], D = [0].

Link to the circuit. s² + (R/L)s + 1/(LC) = s² + 3s + 2, the same polynomial: the eigenvalues of A are the natural frequencies. Both are real and negative, so the response is overdamped (α = 1.5 > ω₀ = √2 = 1.41).
Final state for a 1 V step. Set ẋ = 0: 2iL = 0 gives iL(∞) = 0, and −3(0) − vC + 1 = 0 gives vC(∞) = 1 V. Then y = vL(∞) = −3(0) − 1 + 1 = 0 ✓ (an inductor carries no voltage in DC steady state).

answer.text: Step response from the state model. With x(0) = 0 and u = 1 V, the solution has the modes e−t and e−2t:
answer.pre:
v<sub>C</sub>(t) = 1 − 2e<sup>−t</sup> + e<sup>−2t</sup>
i<sub>L</sub>(t) = C dv<sub>C</sub>/dt = e<sup>−t</sup> − e<sup>−2t</sup>
y = v<sub>L</sub>(t) = 1 − 3i<sub>L</sub> − v<sub>C</sub> = −e<sup>−t</sup> + 2e<sup>−2t</sup>

answer: Check. At t = 0.5 s: RiL + vL + vC = 0.716 + 0.129 + 0.155 = 1.0 V ✓.

answer.text: Transfer function from the state model. H(s) = C(sI − A)⁻¹B + D. Here (sI − A)⁻¹B = [s; 2]/(s² + 3s + 2), so:
answer.pre:
y = v<sub>C</sub>:  H(s) = 2/(s² + 3s + 2)
y = v<sub>L</sub>:  H(s) = (−3s − 2)/(s² + 3s + 2) + 1 = s²/(s² + 3s + 2)

answer: Check by impedances. VL/Vs = sL/(R + sL + 1/(sC)) = s/(3 + s + 2/s) = s²/(s² + 3s + 2) ✓.
Common slips. Choosing a resistor current as a state (it is not an energy variable and can jump); losing the 1/C in dvC/dt = iL/C; and setting D = 0 for an output that the source reaches directly.
Initial output. From rest, x(0) = 0, so y(0⁺) = Du = 1 V: the whole step appears across L at once, as the initial-condition rules predict.

bank.q: Define the network function of a circuit. For a series RLC circuit with R = 2 Ω, L = 1 H and C = 0.2 F, with the output taken across R, find H(s) = V<sub>R</sub>(s)/V<sub>s</sub>(s), draw its pole-zero plot, judge its stability, find its impulse response, and find |H(jω)| at ω = 0, 1, √5 and 4 rad/s.
outline: H(s) = Y(s)/X(s) with independent sources killed and zero initial conditions
Zero at s = 0; poles −1 ± j2; all poles in the left half-plane: stable
h(t) = e<sup>−t</sup>(2 cos 2t − sin 2t) for t ≥ 0
answer: Definition. A network function is H(s) = Y(s)/X(s): the transform of one chosen response divided by the transform of one excitation, with all other independent sources killed and all initial conditions zero. If input and output share a port it is a driving-point function; otherwise a transfer function.

answer.pre:
H(s) = R / (R + sL + 1/(sC)) = R s C / (LC s² + RC s + 1)
     = (R/L) s / (s² + (R/L) s + 1/(LC))
     = 2s / (s² + 2s + 5)

answer: Zeros and poles. Numerator 2s: one zero at s = 0. Denominator s² + 2s + 5 = (s + 1)² + 4: poles at s = −1 ± j2.

answer.text: Pole-zero plot. × at −1 + j2 and −1 − j2, ○ at the origin.

svg.aria: Pole-zero plot with a zero at the origin and poles at minus 1 plus and minus j2.
svg.body: <line x1="220" y1="110" x2="500" y2="110" style="stroke:var(--line2);stroke-width:1.5" marker-end="url(#ar-UID-m)"/><line x1="400" y1="210" x2="400" y2="12" style="stroke:var(--line2);stroke-width:1.5" marker-end="url(#ar-UID-m)"/><text x="496" y="132" font-size="15" text-anchor="end" style="fill:var(--muted)" font-style="italic">σ</text><text x="408" y="24" font-size="15" text-anchor="start" style="fill:var(--muted)" font-style="italic">jω</text><circle cx="400" cy="110" r="8" style="fill:var(--fig);stroke:var(--next);stroke-width:2.5"/><line x1="353" y1="33" x2="367" y2="47" style="stroke:var(--accent);stroke-width:3"/><line x1="353" y1="47" x2="367" y2="33" style="stroke:var(--accent);stroke-width:3"/><line x1="353" y1="173" x2="367" y2="187" style="stroke:var(--accent);stroke-width:3"/><line x1="353" y1="187" x2="367" y2="173" style="stroke:var(--accent);stroke-width:3"/><text x="342" y="45" font-size="13" text-anchor="end" style="fill:var(--accent)" font-weight="700">−1 + j2</text><text x="342" y="185" font-size="13" text-anchor="end" style="fill:var(--accent)" font-weight="700">−1 − j2</text><text x="414" y="132" font-size="13" text-anchor="start" style="fill:var(--next)" font-weight="700">zero at 0</text><line x1="360" y1="106" x2="360" y2="114" style="stroke:var(--line2);stroke-width:1.5"/><text x="360" y="132" font-size="13" text-anchor="middle" style="fill:var(--muted)">−1</text>

answer: Stability. Both poles have real part −1 < 0, so every natural term decays: the circuit is stable. The zero at the origin does not affect stability; it only says the circuit passes no DC (the capacitor blocks it).

answer.text: Impulse response. Complete the square and use the shifted pairs:
answer.pre:
H(s) = 2s/((s + 1)² + 4) = 2(s + 1)/((s + 1)² + 2²) − 2/((s + 1)² + 2²)
h(t) = 2e<sup>−t</sup> cos 2t − e<sup>−t</sup> sin 2t = e<sup>−t</sup>(2 cos 2t − sin 2t),  t ≥ 0

answer: Check by the initial value theorem. h(0⁺) = lim sH(s) as s → ∞ = lim 2s²/(s² + 2s + 5) = 2, and the formula gives e⁰(2 − 0) = 2 ✓.

answer.text: Bandwidth. The half-power points solve |H| = 0.707, that is 5 − ω² = ±2ω:

answer: Sketch of |H(jω)|. Zero at ω = 0, rising through 0.447 at 1 rad/s to the peak of 1 at 2.236 rad/s, then falling (0.588 at 4 rad/s) towards zero as the inductor blocks high frequencies.
Step response. For a 1 V step, VR(s) = H(s)/s = 2/((s + 1)² + 2²), so vR(t) = e−t sin 2t V. It starts at 0, peaks at 0.514 V at t = 0.554 s and dies away: the capacitor blocks the step in the end.
Phase. ∠H(jω) = 90° − tan⁻¹(2ω/(5 − ω²)): +63.4° at 1 rad/s (the capacitor dominates, current leads), 0° at √5 rad/s and −54.0° at 4 rad/s (the inductor dominates).

Reading. The response is zero at DC (the zero at the origin), rises to 1 at the resonant frequency ω₀ = 1/√(LC) = √5 rad/s, where L and C cancel and all of Vs appears across R, and falls again: a band-pass network. The poles lie at distance √5 from the origin, the same ω₀, and their real part −1 = −R/(2L) sets the bandwidth R/L = 2 rad/s.

bank.q: Explain the Laplace transform method for a circuit with one inductor and one capacitor, stating where the initial conditions enter and how the answer is checked. Apply it: a series RLC circuit with R = 3 Ω, L = 1 H and C = 0.5 F has i<sub>L</sub>(0⁻) = 1 A and v<sub>C</sub>(0⁻) = 2 V, and a 10 V step is applied at t = 0. Find i(t) and v<sub>C</sub>(t).
outline: Find i<sub>L</sub>(0⁻), v<sub>C</sub>(0⁻) from the t < 0 circuit
Models: sL with series source L i<sub>L</sub>(0⁻); 1/(sC) with series source v<sub>C</sub>(0⁻)/s
KVL or KCL in s; solve; partial fractions; invert
answer: Step 1, initial state. Solve the circuit for t < 0 (DC: L short, C open) to get iL(0⁻) and vC(0⁻). Here they are given: 1 A and 2 V.
Step 2, transform the sources. A DC source V becomes V/s; here 10/s.

Step 3, transform the elements. R → R. L → sL in series with a source L iL(0⁻), which drives current in the direction iL already had. C → 1/(sC) in series with a source vC(0⁻)/s, which opposes current entering its + plate. This is where the initial conditions enter.

answer.text: Step 4, KVL in s. sL = s, 1/(sC) = 2/s, L iL(0⁻) = 1, vC(0⁻)/s = 2/s:

answer: Step 6, invert. i(t) = 7e−t − 6e−2t A for t ≥ 0.
Final value theorem. sVC(s) → 10 as s → 0, valid because the poles −1 and −2 of sVC(s) are in the left half-plane ✓.
Inductor voltage. vL = L di/dt = −7e−t + 12e−2t V. At t = 0.5 s: i = 2.038 A, vC = 3.716 V and vL = 0.169 V, and 3 × 2.038 + 0.169 + 3.716 = 10.0 V ✓ (KVL holds at every instant).

Parallel form. The same circuit can be solved with Norton models: L becomes sL in parallel with iL(0⁻)/s and C becomes 1/(sC) in parallel with C vC(0⁻). Use the series forms for mesh equations and the parallel forms for nodal equations.

Common slips. Writing C vC(0⁻) in series in place of vC(0⁻)/s; giving the inductor source the wrong sign (it must keep iL flowing the way it was); and inverting before checking that the fraction is proper.

answer.text: Zero-input and zero-state parts. Split I(s) by its causes:

answer: Reading. Both parts have the same two modes, e−t and e−2t, because the poles belong to the circuit; the source and the stored energy only set how much of each mode appears.
Character. The poles −1 and −2 are the roots of s² + 3s + 2 = s² + (R/L)s + 1/(LC), so the circuit is overdamped (α = 1.5 > ω₀ = 1.41): no ringing, as the answer shows.

glossary.def: The part of a response that dies away with time after a change in the circuit.
The condition reached after the transient has vanished, when every quantity repeats or stays constant.
An abrupt change in the circuit at t = 0, usually by closing or opening a switch.
A fall of the form Ae<sup>−t/τ</sup>, in which equal time steps give equal fractional drops.
The value τ in e<sup>−t/τ</sup>; the time for the response to fall to 36.8% of its starting value.
The response of a circuit after its source is removed, driven only by stored energy.
The response produced by the circuit's own poles with independent sources set to zero.
The response forced by the source, equal to the steady state for DC and sine inputs.
The polynomial equation whose roots are the natural frequencies of the circuit.
A value of s that makes the natural response possible; written s₁ and s₂ for a second-order circuit.
The loss of oscillatory energy caused by resistance, which makes a second-order response settle.
A second-order case with two distinct real roots; the response settles without oscillating.
The boundary case with equal real roots; the fastest settling without overshoot.
A second-order case with complex roots; the response oscillates while it decays.
The dimensionless number α/ω<sub>n</sub> that measures how strongly oscillation is suppressed.
The frequency in rad/s at which the circuit would oscillate with no resistance.
The actual oscillation frequency ω<sub>n</sub>√(1 − ζ²) when the circuit is underdamped.
A rule that maps a time function f(t) to a complex-frequency function F(s).
The step that recovers f(t) from F(s), usually by partial fractions and a table.
Splitting a ratio of polynomials into simple terms whose inverse transforms are known.
The ratio Y(s)/X(s) of output to input transform for zero initial energy.
A value of s where the transfer function becomes infinite and the natural response lives.
A value of s where the transfer function becomes zero, blocking transmission at that frequency.
The output when the input is a unit impulse; it is the inverse Laplace transform of H(s).
The complex plane with σ on the horizontal axis and jω on the vertical axis, used to plot poles and zeros.
One of the minimum set of quantities, here i<sub>L</sub> and v<sub>C</sub>, that fixes the future behaviour of the circuit.
